description.p: Locus is a system monitor for Wayland desktops, built with GTK 4 and libadwaita. It lists the running apps and processes with what each takes of the processor, the memory, the disks and the graphics card, and graphs the whole machine.

ul.li: Running apps with their processes, and every other process, tinted by what each uses, sorted by any column and searchable by name, command line or ID
End, kill, stop and continue a process, or end an app with all its processes
A pane with the threads, open files, network connections and priority of what is selected
Services of the machine and the user, which can be started, stopped and restarted, with their logs
Apps that start with the session, how long the last boot took and the services that took longest
A page and a small graph for the processor, memory, each disk, each network connection and each graphics card, reaching back up to 5 minutes

description.p: Everything but services is read from /proc and /sys, and processes are read only while something on screen shows them.

screenshot.caption: Find the apps and processes that keep the machine busy
Watch the processor over the last minutes, and see what is using it
Follow each graphics card's usage, video memory and temperature
Start, stop and read the logs of services
Choose what starts with the session and see how long the last boot took

description.p: Locus does much less work to stay open. Reading the processes costs a fraction of what it did, file systems are read only while their page is shown, and a hidden window no longer updates what nobody can see. The window fills in at once on launch, with the processor, network and disk figures following a moment later. Processes showing the same processor use keep their places instead of swapping on every update, and the process list holds less memory. A process that starts using a graphics card can take a few updates to show it in the GPU column.

The first release: running apps and processes with their processor, memory, disk and graphics card use, which can be ended, killed, stopped and continued; graphs of the processor, each of its cores, memory and swap, the network, the disks and the graphics cards; and the room left on each mounted disk.
